message.content:
Nicolaus Copernicus faced significant opposition from Aristotelian-Ptolemaic scholars when he published *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* in 1543. The Catholic Church later formally condemned the Copernican system, though this official stance solidified in the decades following his death. Many contemporary astronomers criticized his heliocentrism as physically implausible, arguing that Earth's motion contradicted common sense and the established framework of Aristotelian physics.

Why would a respected canon of the Church dare to upend 1,400 years of Ptolemaic tradition? How could one account for the apparent stillness of the firmament if the Earth were actually in motion? Was the opposition purely scientific, or was it deeply rooted in theological discomfort?

How radical was it to declare that the Sun, not the Earth, stood at the center of everything! What a profound challenge to the very foundations of natural philosophy his work posed! How could anyone accept that the sky above their heads was not fixed and unchanging?
